title: The Voder, the first electronic voice
hook: At the 1939 World's Fair, women played speech on a keyboard like an organ.
peek: Bell Labs' Voder made speech from pure electricity. A trained operator pressed keys and a foot pedal to shape buzzes and hisses into words, live, in front of crowds at the 1939 World's Fair. Learning to play it took months of practice.
lede: Talking machines are older than electricity: in the 1700s Wolfgang von Kempelen built one with bellows and a leather mouth. The Voder, shown by Bell Labs at the 1939 New York World's Fair, was the first to make speech electronically. It had no recordings inside. A trained operator built every word by hand, in real time, the way a pianist builds a chord.

bullets.text: The Bell Labs engineer Homer Dudley built the Voder from his earlier vocoder, which split the voice into frequency bands. The Voder ran this idea in reverse, starting with a buzz or a hiss and shaping it into vowels and consonants.

Ten finger keys controlled ten bands of sound. A wrist bar switched between a voiced buzz and a breathy hiss, extra keys made sounds like p and k, and a foot pedal raised and lowered the pitch so sentences could rise into questions.

Bell Labs trained a team of young women, mostly telephone operators, to play it. Training took months, by some accounts a year. At the fair a host would ask for a phrase, and the operator made the machine say it, even changing the tune of a sentence to alter its meaning.

The Voder itself was soon retired, but the vocoder idea lived on. Decades later musicians used vocoders to make robotic singing voices, a sound that traces back to Dudley's work on squeezing speech down telephone lines.
